observation: Inference providers must keep many LLMs available, including low-volume but essential models, while token prices fall, making resource efficiency increasingly important. To meet strict SLOs they dedicate GPU groups per model, yet production GPU duty cycles commonly fall below 30%. Analyses of production traces from major inference providers (Hyperbolic, Novita AI) and Chatbot Arena reveal a dynamic, rapidly shifting bursty-group pattern: requests concentrate on a small subset of concurrently active models and that subset changes frequently (23%–50% of models active on average; active set changes 54–766 times per hour), and per-model request streams are extremely volatile with abrupt pattern shifts and many idle intervals. In such conditions pure time sharing causes repeated model swapping, thrashing, and SLO-violating queuing spikes, while pure space sharing leaves memory locked to idle models (in the Novita AI trace models are idle over 70% of the time and roughly 50% of GPU memory is occupied but unused), starving active models during bursts. Thus neither sharing strategy alone can satisfy SLOs and efficiency under realistic multi-LLM workloads; what is needed is a fluid combination of both.

claims: Continuous batching and paged KV-cache management are the core techniques used by modern LLM serving stacks to improve GPU utilization while honoring latency constraints for a single generative model.
These systems are per-model serving engines: they assume that one model's weights and KV cache remain resident on preassigned GPUs, and they do not make cross-model placement or eviction decisions.

works.title: Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models
Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention

claims: Cluster-level prediction-serving frameworks have optimized model placement and autoscaling across multiple DNN models to meet latency SLOs with minimal GPU cost.
AlpaServe shows that statistical multiplexing of bursty inference request streams can be combined with model parallelism to improve serving efficiency across multiple models.

These frameworks approach GPU sharing as a capacity-planning problem and largely assume that model weights are already placed on selected replicas, rather than modeling the cost of repeatedly swapping full LLM weights in and out of GPU memory.

works.title: InferLine: Latency-aware Provisioning and Resource Scaling for Prediction Serving
AlpaServe: Statistical Multiplexing with Model Parallelism for Deep Learning Serving

claims: Recent multi-LLM serving systems have explicitly examined how to colocate different generative models on the same GPUs, identifying spatial partitioning and temporal sharing as the two fundamental multiplexing dimensions.
MuxServe demonstrates that flexibly mixing spatial GPU partitions and temporal model slots can meet latency objectives with far fewer GPUs than either pure time sharing or pure space sharing alone.

Adapter-oriented serving systems reduce the marginal memory cost of many models by sharing one resident base model, but they apply only to closely coupled checkpoint variants and not to a catalog of distinct pretrained LLMs.

works.title: MuxServe: Flexible Spatial-Temporal Multiplexing for Multiple LLM Serving
S-LoRA: Serving Thousands of Concurrent LoRA Adapters

solution.idea: The prior approaches each optimize one side of the multiplexing problem. Per-model serving engines such as those from continuous batching and paged KV-cache work are effective only after a model is resident on a GPU; they never decide whether that model should be resident or swapped out. Cluster-level placement and autoscaling frameworks view the problem as capacity planning, assuming weights are already placed on selected replicas and ignoring the time and resource cost of repeatedly moving multi-GB LLM weights. MuxServe is the right starting point because it treats spatial partitions and temporal slots as commensurable resources, but the challenge posed by the observation is that the optimal mix is not a fixed or slowly varying configuration: the active set is small, shifts dozens to hundreds of times per hour, and individual streams have many idle intervals. A static or periodic derivation of a spatial/temporal schedule will either lock memory to models that have gone idle or load and evict models too late, causing SLO-violating queuing spikes. The key insight is to stop viewing space and time sharing as two modes of a GPU and instead view the GPU memory region occupied by a model as a lifecycle state with a continuously adjustable retention value. Each loaded model instance is in one of several states: a core resident model is treated as always resident and serves requests without load latency; a shadow model is loaded in free or reusable memory as an opportunity cost, serving requests if they arrive soon but being evictable first when memory is needed; a scheduled transient model is loaded only for a predicted or observed burst and is boundary-swapped by the scheduler. The fluidity comes from the planner deciding, for every model replica, how long it should stay in memory and what priority it has relative to the next predicted active group. Core residents provide the space-sharing backbone that absorbs the stable part of the trace and prevents repeated swapping for models whose active windows recur faster than the swap cost. Scheduled transient slots provide time sharing for rare or newly emerging models and avoid permanently reserving memory for them. Shadow occupancy fills the spaces left by both, making memory useful without committing to a model, and it gives the scheduler a set of already-warm candidate weights so that an active-set change can often be served by promoting a shadow model rather than by a cold load. The planner explicitly trades off three costs: the memory cost of keeping a model resident while idle, the transfer cost of loading it from host or storage, and the SLO cost of not having it ready when a burst starts. This turns the problem into a cache-replacement problem over model weights, where a model is retained if the expected benefit of avoiding future load latency exceeds the expected memory opportunity cost. A model whose benefit crosses below the eviction threshold is demoted to shadow and then evicted only when a higher-benefit model needs the memory; this hysteresis prevents thrashing under noisy idle intervals. The alternatives I considered were a purely reactive least-recently-used weight cache, a purely predictive reservation of the predicted active set, and a fixed ratio of spatial partitions to temporal slots. Purely reactive caching fails because it swaps at the first idle request and is fooled by abrupt bursts; purely predictive reservation fails because the active set changes too quickly and the forecast horizon is shorter than load time on many shifts; a fixed ratio fails because the mix must depend on bursty-group dynamics. I rejected adapter-based weight sharing because it only works for closely coupled checkpoint variants, whereas the catalog contains distinct pretrained models. The resulting design is a hybrid controller built on top of per-model batching engines: it reuses MuxServe's idea of comparing spatial and temporal placements in one objective, but it makes the placement update online at the timescale of active-set changes and treats weight transfer as a first-class scheduling action rather than an unmodeled startup cost.
solution.implementation:
The implementation is a cluster-wide control plane plus a data plane of per-GPU workers. Each GPU worker can host multiple model serving slices. A slice is a self-contained continuous-batching engine with paged KV-cache memory, i.e., a model instance created by loading one model's weights into a contiguous physical or virtual memory region on the GPU. The worker reports to the controller the state of every slice: loading, resident, shadow, draining, idling, or evicted, together with memory usage, queue depth, and effective GPU duty cycle. Model weights are stored on a shared weight store and staged into pinned host memory; the controller initiates asynchronous DMA transfers into a chosen GPU memory region, and new arrivals are routed to the slice only after the loading state completes.

The controller maintains a small set of statistics per model and per GPU. For each short observation window T_obs (e.g., 1 second), it records the number of arrivals for each model and the number of active seconds. A model is considered active in that window if its arrival rate exceeds a small threshold theta_active. These active vectors are fed to an online co-activation tracker. The tracker keeps an exponentially decaying affinity matrix whose entry aff[m][n] is the fraction of recent windows in which models m and n were active together. From the affinity matrix, the controller extracts a small number of recurrent active groups by a connected-components or maximum-weight clique approximation; this is not a one-time clustering but is updated continuously so that when the active set starts to shift from group G_old to group G_new, the controller already has a probabilistic forecast of the next active set and its likely transition time. The controller also computes, for each model, an idle-gap predictor: a distribution of intervals between active windows, represented by exponentially weighted mean and variance. This predictor is used to estimate whether a model that just became idle is worth retaining.

Every T_replan seconds (e.g., every 2 seconds) and whenever the active-group tracker detects a statistically significant change of active set, the planner runs. The planner first scores every model that is currently loaded or likely to be loaded. The score is the expected marginal benefit of keeping that model resident for the next planning horizon, benefit_m = saved_load_latency_m + slo_miss_risk_m - idle_opportunity_cost_m. saved_load_latency_m is estimated as the expected number of arrivals during the horizon times the expected load delay that would be incurred if the model were not resident. slo_miss_risk_m is the probability that those arrivals would violate their SLO because of load delay, weighted by the number of queued requests and their remaining deadlines. idle_opportunity_cost_m is the expected number of idle GPU-memory-seconds the model would occupy if retained, converted to the cost of not being able to load another model in that memory. The planner orders all candidate models by this score and greedily fills each GPU's resident core pool until either the score becomes negative or the core pool memory budget is reached. The core pool budget is computed as the total GPU memory minus a per-GPU reserve Rsv. Rsv is not a static fixed amount; it is the memory currently committed to shadow models and scheduled transient loads. Thus the planner simultaneously chooses how large the core pool is: when many high-benefit models compete for memory, Rsv shrinks and previously shadow models are evicted; when few core models are active, Rsv grows and the controller can fill it with shadow models from the predicted next group.

After core resident assignments are chosen, the planner handles the non-core models that appear in the current or predicted active groups. For each such model, it determines whether the model should be loaded into a shadow slot or scheduled as a transient slot. A model is shadow-loaded if the idle-gap predictor says that, although it is not in the core set, it is likely to become active again before a cold load could complete. Shadow models do not receive a guaranteed serving budget; they are simply memory-resident and can serve requests at no load delay, but they are the first candidates for eviction when memory pressure increases. A model is scheduled as a transient slot if it has accumulated enough queued work that a load is amortized or if its predicted burst is imminent. The planner computes the number of requests that can be served during one activation of that model using the profiled throughput of a slice, and it schedules a time interval on the least-loaded GPU that has enough memory. If no GPU has enough free memory, the planner will not load a brand-new schedule immediately; instead it finds the lowest-score loaded model among shadow and then resident models, marks that model draining, waits for its queued requests to drain for at most drain_ms, and then evicts or, if the victim is still valuable, demotes it to shadow in a smaller or another memory region. Draining prevents SLO violations for requests already accepted by the victim; new requests for the victim are redirected to an activation queue or to another existing slice if one exists.

A central design detail is the state transition path for resident models. When a core model's activity decays, it is not immediately evicted at the end of the active window. Instead the controller demotes it to shadow while keeping its weights in memory. Demotion is a logical change: the model continues to serve any already enqueued requests, but the controller lowers its retention priority and stops advertising it as a guaranteed-resident model. The model remains shadow until either its score rises again and it is promoted back to core, or a higher-benefit model needs its memory and the eviction protocol completes. This hysteresis is essential to avoid thrashing under volatile per-model streams with many idle intervals. A pure time-sharing system would evict the weights as soon as the stream goes idle and then pay load latency at the next burst; a pure space-sharing system would keep the weights forever. Shadow retention sits in between: the controller keeps a model loaded across short idle gaps but releases it before long idle gaps waste memory. The exact decision is governed by the idle-gap predictor and by a per-model retention threshold chosen so that the expected load cost equals the expected cost of holding the memory.

Router policy works as follows. Each incoming request has a model ID and a deadline or SLO class. The router first checks the controller's placement table. If the model has a resident or shadow slice whose local queue depth is below a high-water mark, the request is appended to that slice's continuous-batching queue. If the model has no loaded slice, the request is placed in an activation queue and a wake-up signal is sent to the planner. The wake-up signal carries queue length, earliest deadline, and model ID. The planner uses this signal as an additional input to its next immediate schedule decision. If the activation queue's oldest request already has insufficient slack to wait for a load, the controller escalates the request priority and, if necessary, selects a shadow model or an idling transient slot to evict first. The scheduler never drops requests; in the worst case it allows a short load-induced delay but tries to minimize the number of such events by having shadow models ready. During a time-shared transient activation, the slice runs with continuous batching, and requests are processed in arrival order unless an earlier-deadline request from the activation queue arrives. After the transient model's predicted burst has drained, the model is placed in the idle state; if no immediate next burst is predicted, it is marked shadow and eventually evicted by the same policy.

The planner also performs prefetch scheduling for active-set transitions. When the co-activation tracker announces that the current group is likely to be replaced by a new group, the controller computes the set difference between the two groups. For models entering the new group that are not already loaded, it attempts to start loading their weights into available shadow or reserve memory before the transition completes. This load may be concurrent with serving the outgoing group on other slices of the same GPU, because each GPU can host multiple slices and loads occur into memory regions that are not occupied by executing cores. If the total incoming model weights exceed the reserve memory, the controller chooses a subset to load via a knapsack over weights and predicted transition urgency; the remaining models are scheduled as transient slots immediately after the transition. This prefetch is what smooths the rapid active-set changes: instead of the whole cluster stopping to swap models, each GPU is always consuming or preparing the next workload while still finishing the current one.

Several parameters and structures are required by an implementation. T_obs is the finest observation granularity, typically around 1 second; T_replan is the periodic scheduling granularity, typically 2-5 seconds; theta_active is the minimum request rate at which a model is considered active, set low enough to catch bursts but high enough to suppress noise; Rsv is the dynamic reserve memory measured in bytes, bounded below by the largest expected transient checkpoint plus a small margin; drain_ms is the maximum time the scheduler waits for a draining slice before forced eviction; min_demote_hysteresis is the minimum number of consecutive idle windows a shadow model must experience before it becomes evictable; and load_amortization_threshold is the minimum queued work (in token-seconds) required before the planner will cold-load a model that is not predicted to be in the next group. The per-model profiling function gives the relationship among memory footprint, batch size, and achieved SLO to determine how many requests a transient slot can serve before the model should be released. All state is versioned so that a reconfiguration command only takes effect when the affected slice reaches a safe preemption point, and the router uses the version to avoid sending requests to a stale placement after a model has begun draining. The complete system is therefore a closed loop: continuous-batching engines provide high throughput for a single model while resident; the controller continually re-evaluates which models deserve resident memory, which can be shadowed, and which should be swapped on demand; the co-activation predictor anticipates group changes and prefetches candidate weights; and the drain/demote/evict protocol prevents reactive swapping from destroying SLOs. This directly addresses the observation because the volatile, low-duty-cycle nature of real multi-LLM workloads is treated as the normal operating point rather than as an exception: most memory is used by core models when a stable burst is present, by shadow models during short idle intervals, and by scheduled transient loads during predictable switches, with the balance among these states recomputed continuously as the active set shifts.
